title: Out-of-date adrenaline
topic: Raising concerns about systems and safety
stem:
You are an F2 doctor working an evening shift for the GP out-of-hours service, doing home visits with a driver. Before setting off, you check the emergency drug bag in the car and find that the adrenaline for anaphylaxis expired two months ago.

The bag has a signed checklist saying it was checked last week. Your first visit is waiting.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Set off now and collect new adrenaline when you return to base.
options.brief: You would be without working adrenaline during your visits.
options.detailed: Your first patient is waiting, but an emergency could arise on any visit. A few minutes now is better than being unable to treat anaphylaxis.

options.text: Note the expiry on the checklist so the next shift sees it.
options.brief: A note may help later, but it doesn't make tonight's bag safe or explain the failure.
options.detailed: Recording what you found has some value, but it leaves you without working adrenaline tonight and doesn't trigger any review of why the check missed it.

options.text: Tell your driver so he can mention it to whoever restocks the cars.
options.brief: An informal message may never reach the right person.
options.detailed: Passing it on informally doesn't make sure it is fixed or reviewed, and it relies on someone else remembering.

options.text: Find out who signed the checklist and confront them about it.
options.brief: Confrontation isn't the way to deal with a system failure.
options.detailed: The person who signed may have made an honest mistake, or the system may be at fault. The incident process is the right route for finding out what happened.

options.text: Get in-date adrenaline from the base before setting off.
options.brief: You may need it on any visit, so it must be replaced now.
options.detailed: Anaphylaxis can occur at any time, and expired adrenaline may not work. Replacing it before you leave takes a few minutes and means you are equipped for an emergency.

options.text: Check the expiry dates of the rest of the drugs in the bag.
options.brief: If one item was missed, others may have been too.
options.detailed: The checklist was signed, yet expired adrenaline was missed. Other drugs in the bag may also be out of date, so a quick check protects patients on tonight's visits.

options.text: Email the service's pharmacist next week about stock checks.
options.brief: Too slow, and it doesn't deal with tonight's risk.
options.detailed: Contacting pharmacy may be useful, but waiting a week leaves the problem in place, and it doesn't address tonight's shift.

options.text: Report the expired drug and the signed check as an incident.
options.brief: A signed check that missed an expired drug is a system problem to review.
options.detailed: The checking process failed, which may affect other cars too. Reporting it lets the service review how bags are checked. The aim is learning, not blame.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you deal with an immediate equipment risk and also report a failed safety check.
explanation.keyDetails: The adrenaline has expired. The bag was signed as checked. You are about to start visits. Replacing it takes minutes.
explanation.reasoning: [E] fixes the immediate risk, [F] checks for other gaps, and [H] reports the failure so it can be reviewed. The distractors leave you without a working drug ([A], [B]), rely on informal messages ([C], [G]), or confront rather than report ([D]).
explanation.competing: [A] is tempting because a patient is waiting, but the delay to replace the adrenaline is short and the risk of not having it is serious.

references.title: Good medical practice
references.note: Domain 3, acting on risks to patient safety.

references.title: Patient Safety Incident Response Framework
references.note: Reporting incidents so systems can be improved.
